summary:
Guernsey is a self-governing Crown Dependency with its own parliament, the States of Guernsey, and its own statute book. The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and the single-sex-services code issued under it in 2025 do not apply here automatically. Local law governs, and United Kingdom measures reach Guernsey only by Order in Council.

On 10 December 2015 the States approved same-sex marriage by 37 votes to 7. Two alternatives were put and rejected as insufficient: a civil-partnership-only scheme, and a single secular status called Union Civile that would have applied to all couples alike. The enabling legislation was left to a separate bill, which commenced in 2018.

Family recognition moved earlier the same year. A review of the Adoption Law recorded at page 1170 of the States of Guernsey Billet d'État of 24 June 2015 ended a fifty-year bar on unmarried couples adopting. The States agreed that same-sex couples may adopt, that civil partnerships are recognised for that purpose, and that both partners hold equal parental responsibility.

No source establishes legal gender recognition or trans-specific protection in force in Guernsey.
tangentialFactors:
Guernsey's reforms of the 2010s track the United Kingdom closely rather than running ahead of it. On 23 September 2011 the island adopted the United Kingdom's relaxed blood-donor rules, with the local change targeted for about 7 November 2011 to match the United Kingdom's own timetable. Gay and bisexual men became eligible after a twelve-month deferral, ending a local ban dating from the 1980s HIV era; other donation restrictions were left unchanged.

The adoption reform belonged to a small regional pattern. Jersey's assembly approved the same change two days before Guernsey's, and the two jurisdictions moved in the same session of work rather than one following the other.

Organised opposition at the marriage debate was thin. The charity Liberate called it a historic day, and the States debate was described as extremely positive before the 37-7 result.
localsOnly:
Residents adopting in Guernsey are assessed under the amended Adoption Law, which recognises civil partnerships and assigns equal parental responsibility to both partners of a couple.

Local blood services apply a twelve-month deferral to gay and bisexual donors alongside the standard donor restrictions. The 1980s-era exclusion is no longer in force.

Les Nicolles, opened in 1989, is Guernsey's only prison. It is operated by the States of Guernsey, has 11 wings and a capacity of 139, and accommodates male, female and vulnerable prisoners of juvenile and adult ages. The population stood at about 99 in November 2024.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source establishes a legal gender-recognition mechanism in Guernsey, and none establishes trans-specific anti-discrimination protection in force. Whether local equality law covers gender identity on the same footing as sexual orientation is not sourced here and remains unresolved.

The material reviewed on Les Nicolles contains no rule for housing trans prisoners by birth sex or identified gender, no trans-specific unit, and no stated solitary or segregation practice for trans prisoners. Nothing on the prison-housing axis can be verified from it.

No Order in Council extending the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 to Guernsey appears in the sources reviewed, so the Act and its 2025 single-sex-services code are treated as not applying. Confirming the absence of such an order is a research task still outstanding.
